ROBOTICS DEEP MASTER CORPUS — 3,390 EXAMPLES
================================================

EXPANSION BASIS
---------------
This corpus expands the supplied K–12 → B.Tech/B.E. → M.Tech/M.S. robotics
curriculum into a large machine-learning/research-oriented corpus.

DOMAINS
-------
Foundations, mechanics, electronics, embedded systems, sensors, actuators,
mobile robotics, rigid-body mathematics, transformations, kinematics,
Jacobians, dynamics, PID/control, state estimation, trajectory generation,
computer vision, LiDAR, sensor fusion, localization, SLAM, navigation,
ROS 2, simulation, manipulation, force control, MPC, reinforcement learning,
legged robotics, humanoids, UAVs, industrial robotics, medical robotics,
soft/swarm robotics, safety, cybersecurity, autonomous logistics, modern
robotics AI, research methodology and capstone design.

EXACT TOTAL: 3,390 EXAMPLES.

Each example includes:
CONCEPT → ROBOT CONTEXT → ENGINEERING MODEL → CODE → CASE STUDY →
IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS → FAILURE MODES → VALIDATION → ADVANCED EXTENSION →
RESEARCH EXTENSION → CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION.

Numerical values are illustrative engineering examples and are not safety
certification limits or guaranteed hardware specifications.

CORE LOOP
---------
SENSE → ESTIMATE → PLAN → CONTROL → ACT → OBSERVE → UPDATE

EXAMPLE 0001 | Robotics Foundations & Robot Anatomy | torque-speed tradeoff
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

CONCEPT
-------
Study torque-speed tradeoff as a component of a complete robotic system. The local concept
must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: 6-DOF manipulator
Representative mass: 9 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.170 m
Representative speed: 0.210 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.028 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 9 × 9.81 × 0.170 × 1.4
≈ 21.013 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 0.296706 rad
current = 0.201760 rad
error = target − current = 0.094946 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 9
lever_arm = 0.170
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.4

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 0.296706
current = 0.201760
error = target - current
kp = 1.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using torque-speed tradeoff during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect torque-speed tradeoff with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

-----------------
Consider a robot using loop closure during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds

actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

------------------

hardware gap.

• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: industrial robot
Representative mass: 51 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.870 m
Representative speed: 0.170 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.046 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 51 × 9.81 × 0.870 × 1.8
≈ 783.485 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 3.473205 rad
current = 2.257583 rad
error = target − current = 1.215622 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 51
lever_arm = 0.870
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.8

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 3.473205
current = 2.257583
error = target - current
kp = 4.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using multi-robot coordination during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect multi-robot coordination with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

```python
# Illustrative robotics computation

print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using PRM during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

-----------------------------

• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact

• unsafe state transition

---------------

feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: mobile manipulator
Representative mass: 93 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.570 m
Representative speed: 0.850 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.040 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 93 × 9.81 × 0.570 × 1.4
≈ 728.039 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 6.021386 rad
current = 4.997750 rad
error = target − current = 1.023636 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 93
lever_arm = 0.570
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.4

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 6.021386
current = 4.997750
error = target - current
kp = 3.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using Ackermann steering during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect Ackermann steering with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: 6-DOF manipulator
Representative mass: 9 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.670 m
Representative speed: 0.210 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.028 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 9 × 9.81 × 0.670 × 1.8
≈ 106.478 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 3.961897 rad
current = 2.694090 rad
error = target − current = 1.267807 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 9
lever_arm = 0.670
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.8

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 3.961897
current = 2.694090
error = target - current
kp = 1.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using Newton-Euler dynamics during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

-----------------

τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor

```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
```
```python
mass = 79
lever_arm = 0.370
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.4
```

```python
current = 1.894904

kp = 2.50

print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

-----------------

4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

-------------

• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:

payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

------------------

Study peg-in-hole as a component of a complete robotic system. The local concept

--------------------

Representative speed: 0.710 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.028 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 65 × 9.81 × 0.670 × 1.8
≈ 769.006 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 3.263766 rad
current = 2.317274 rad
error = target − current = 0.946492 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 65
lever_arm = 0.670
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.8

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 3.263766
current = 2.317274
error = target - current
kp = 1.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using peg-in-hole during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

-----------------------------

CONCEPT
-------
Study numerical IK as a component of a complete robotic system. The local concept
must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: quadruped
Representative mass: 2 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.520 m
Representative speed: 1.420 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.031 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 2 × 9.81 × 0.520 × 1.2
≈ 12.243 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 2.513274 rad
current = 1.633628 rad
error = target − current = 0.879646 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 2
lever_arm = 0.520
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.2

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 2.513274
current = 1.633628
error = target - current
kp = 2.00
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using numerical IK during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect numerical IK with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

---------------

• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 16 × 9.81 × 0.120 × 1.2
≈ 22.602 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 2.373648 rad
current = 1.685290 rad
error = target − current = 0.688358 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 16
lever_arm = 0.120
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.2

target = 2.373648
current = 1.685290

kp = 5.00

print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using differential flatness during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and


SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using SLERP during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

-----------------------------

must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: 6-DOF manipulator
Representative mass: 23 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.470 m
Representative speed: 0.110 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.028 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 23 × 9.81 × 0.470 × 1.8
≈ 190.883 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 0.122173 rad
current = 0.090408 rad
error = target − current = 0.031765 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 23
lever_arm = 0.470
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.8

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 0.122173
current = 0.090408
error = target - current
kp = 1.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using stepper motor during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect stepper motor with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: industrial robot
Representative mass: 9 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.170 m
Representative speed: 1.470 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.046 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 9 × 9.81 × 0.170 × 1.4
≈ 21.013 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 1.553343 rad
current = 1.056273 rad
error = target − current = 0.497070 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 9
lever_arm = 0.170
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.4

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 1.553343
current = 1.056273
error = target - current
kp = 4.50
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using world frame during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect world frame with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:

• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------

• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

---------------

Study MPC as a component of a complete robotic system. The local concept
must ultimately connect sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation,
feedback and safety.

REPRESENTATIVE ROBOT
--------------------
Platform: warehouse AMR
Representative mass: 2 kg
Representative lever arm: 0.520 m
Representative speed: 1.300 m/s
Representative wheel radius where applicable: 0.025 m

ENGINEERING MODEL
-----------------
Torque sizing example:
τ ≈ m × g × L × safety factor
≈ 2 × 9.81 × 0.520 × 1.2
≈ 12.243 N·m

Tracking example:
target = 0.000000 rad
current = 0.000000 rad
error = target − current = 0.000000 rad

CODE PATTERN
------------
```python
# Illustrative robotics computation
mass = 2
lever_arm = 0.520
gravity = 9.81
safety_factor = 1.2

required_torque = mass * gravity * lever_arm * safety_factor

target = 0.000000
current = 0.000000
error = target - current
kp = 1.00
control_output = kp * error

print("torque:", required_torque)
print("tracking_error:", error)
print("control_output:", control_output)
```

SYSTEM CASE STUDY
-----------------
Consider a robot using MPC during an autonomous task. Sensor data first
enters the perception/estimation layer. The resulting state estimate feeds
planning or task logic. The controller converts the desired state into
actuator commands. Sensors then measure the response, closing the feedback
loop.

A production implementation should explicitly separate:
1. safety-critical functions,
2. real-time control,
3. state estimation,
4. perception,
5. planning,
6. task-level autonomy,
7. logging and diagnostics.

IMPLEMENTATION QUESTIONS
------------------------
• What are the inputs and outputs?
• Which coordinate frame is used?
• What is the sampling frequency?
• What latency is acceptable?
• What uncertainty exists?
• What calibration is required?
• What happens during sensor dropout?
• What happens during actuator saturation?
• What happens if localization is lost?
• What happens if computation exceeds its deadline?

FAILURE MODES
-------------
• sensor noise or dropout
• timestamp synchronization error
• calibration drift
• actuator saturation
• mechanical backlash
• communication latency
• model mismatch
• unexpected contact
• computational overload
• unsafe state transition

VALIDATION PLAN
---------------
Use quantitative tests appropriate to the subsystem:
trajectory tracking error, localization error, settling time, overshoot,
collision rate, task success rate, energy consumption, latency, repeatability,
payload capacity, recovery rate or estimation error.

ADVANCED EXTENSION
------------------
Implement the subsystem in simulation, introduce realistic sensor noise,
actuator limits and communication latency, then perform hardware-in-the-loop
testing before controlled real-robot experiments. Quantify the simulation-to-
hardware gap.

RESEARCH EXTENSION
------------------
Define a baseline, test protocol, quantitative metrics, ablations, failure
taxonomy and reproducible configuration. Report unsuccessful trials and
uncertainty rather than only successful demonstrations.

CROSS-DISCIPLINARY CONNECTION
-----------------------------
Connect MPC with at least three of:
kinematics, dynamics, control, perception, estimation, planning, embedded
systems, ROS 2, AI, mechanical engineering, safety, simulation or HRI.

```python
print("control_output:", control_output)
```
